title: Challenges to Democracy
subtitle: Narrativ versjon
description: A story about the pressures testing democracy in the 21st century -- populism, polarisation and disinformation -- and why understanding them is the first step to defending it.
competenceGoals: discuss threats to democracy and democratic institutions in the modern world
analyse the impact of social media and disinformation on democratic processes

content.content:
## The end of history that wasn't

When the Cold War ended in 1991, many people believed democracy had simply won. The political scientist Francis Fukuyama famously announced "the end of history," arguing that liberal democracy had triumphed as the final form of human government and would now spread across the globe. Three decades later, that confidence looks misplaced. The watchdog organisation Freedom House has recorded a decline in global freedom for more than fifteen years running, with democratic erosion striking both young and well-established democracies.

Democracy, it turns out, is not invulnerable. It faces a cluster of serious modern challenges -- the rise of populism, deepening polarisation, the flood of disinformation on social media, and a fraying of trust in democratic institutions. Understanding these threats is not a reason for despair. It is the first step toward meeting them, because democracy has weathered crises before and proven remarkably resilient -- but only when citizens understood what they were up against.

## Populism and polarisation: when politics becomes a war

**Populism** is a political approach that frames society as a struggle between "the people" -- pictured as virtuous and united -- and "the elite" -- pictured as corrupt and self-serving. Populist leaders claim to be the single authentic voice of the ordinary citizen against powerful insiders. Its features include hostility to elites, the simplification of complex problems into stories with clear villains, and a suspicion of pluralism that can cast opponents as not truly part of "the people." It is important to be even-handed here: populism appears across the political spectrum. Right-wing populism, such as elements of the Brexit movement or Donald Trump's appeal in the US, often centres on immigration and national identity; left-wing populism, such as Podemos in Spain or Hugo Chavez in Venezuela, often centres on economic inequality and corporate power. Populist movements frequently raise genuine grievances, but the populist *style* can erode democratic norms by attacking the legitimacy of courts and media, treating opponents as enemies, and undermining trust in expertise.

Closely linked is **political polarisation** -- the widening gulf between political camps, where each side sees the other not merely as mistaken but as a threat. As polarisation deepens, compromise gets harder and debate turns hostile. The drivers include social-media algorithms that build echo chambers, partisan media outlets serving one side, economic inequality producing very different life experiences, and politicians who stoke division to rally their base. The United States offers a stark case: surveys show Democrats and Republicans drifting apart ideologically and viewing each other with growing hostility, bipartisan lawmaking has become rare, and in 2020 around 80 percent of voters for each presidential candidate said they had very few or no friends supporting the other. The storming of the US Capitol on 6 January 2021 by supporters who rejected the election result showed, dramatically, where extreme polarisation can lead -- toward strain on the very norms of compromise and peaceful transfer of power that democracy depends on.

content.content:
## Disinformation in the age of the algorithm

The third great pressure is the information environment itself. Two terms matter here. **Disinformation** is false or misleading information spread *deliberately* to deceive, manipulate or cause harm. **Misinformation** is false information spread *without* the intent to deceive -- sharing a rumour you genuinely believe, for instance. Both damage democracy, but disinformation is especially dangerous because it is engineered to exploit divisions and erode trust.

Social media amplifies these threats in several ways. Algorithms create **echo chambers** and **filter bubbles**, feeding people content that confirms what they already believe and shrinking their exposure to other views. False stories often spread faster than true ones because they are more sensational -- a 2018 MIT study found false news on Twitter spread about six times faster than the truth. Foreign actors, such as state-backed troll farms, have used these platforms to meddle in other countries' elections and deepen divisions. As people lose the ability to tell reliable information from fabrication, trust in journalism, science and institutions declines. And new technology raises the stakes further: deepfakes and AI-generated content make convincing fakes ever easier to produce. What can be done? The text points to media-literacy education that teaches people to evaluate sources, greater transparency and responsibility from platforms, support for quality independent journalism, and individual responsibility -- each of us checking before we share. None of this is a silver bullet, but together these responses defend the shared factual ground that democratic debate requires.

questions.task: What is the difference between disinformation and misinformation?

options.text: They are exactly the same thing
Disinformation is only spread by newspapers
Disinformation is spread deliberately to deceive; misinformation is spread without that intent

questions.solution: Disinformation is false information spread deliberately to deceive, while misinformation is false information shared without the intent to mislead.

questions.task: How did a 2018 MIT study describe the spread of false news on Twitter?

options.text: It spread about six times faster than true news
It spread more slowly than true news
It did not spread at all

questions.solution: The study found that false news stories spread roughly six times faster than true ones, partly because they tend to be more sensational.

questions.task: What do filter bubbles and echo chambers do to citizens' information?

options.text: Expose them to a wide range of opposing views
Reinforce existing views and reduce exposure to other perspectives

questions.solution: Filter bubbles and echo chambers show people content aligned with what they already think, reinforcing biases and narrowing their exposure to different views.

questions.task: Which is offered as a way to defend democracy against disinformation?

options.text: Media-literacy education and supporting independent journalism

questions.solution: The chapter suggests media literacy, platform transparency, support for quality journalism and individual responsibility as defences against disinformation.

content.content:
## In short

The optimism of 1991, when democracy seemed destined to spread everywhere, has given way to a sobering reality: global freedom has declined for over fifteen years. Modern democracies face populism, which pits "the people" against "the elite" and exists on both left and right; polarisation, which turns opponents into enemies and makes compromise harder; and disinformation, deliberately false information amplified by social-media algorithms, echo chambers and emerging technologies like deepfakes. These pressures are serious but not unbeatable. Media literacy, support for independent journalism, responsible platforms and engaged, critical citizens are the tools for defending the shared facts and mutual respect that democracy needs. Democracy, as the ancient Athenians understood, is not a spectator sport.
